newsitem.title: DUBAI: Nurses' lawyer says key Saudi trial hearing Sunday.
newsitem.headline: Nurses' lawyer says key Saudi trial hearing Sunday.

text.p: The lawyer of two British nurses on trial for murder in Saudi Arabia said on Wednesday the court would reconvene on Sunday for an important session which could lead to the dismissal of the case.

Salah al-Hejailan, whose firm is defending Lucille McLauchlan and Deborah Parry, said he would meet the nurses' families on Thursday to discuss developments in the case. The court had adjourned on July 7 for deliberation.
"There will be another hearing on Sunday and I expect it will be an important one," Hejailan told Reuters from his hotel suite in London.
"The judges will either display new evidence we haven't yet seen or submit the case to a higher judicial authority. Perhaps the court will nullify the confessions," he said.

Parry, 38, and McLauchlan, 31, have said they were forced into confessing to the murder of Australian colleague Yvonne Gilford at a medical complex in the eastern city of Dhahran in December. Both have since withdrawn the confessions and say they are innocent.
Hejailan, a U.S.-educated lawyer based in Riyadh, has said that if the court in the nearby eastern Saudi city of Khobar nullifies the confessions, it would dismiss the case.
Gilford was found stabbed 13 times, bludgeoned and suffocated in her room at the King Fahd military medical complex just days before her 56th birthday.

If Parry and McLauchlan are found guilty of her murder, they could face the death penalty, which in Saudi Arabia is traditionally public beheading by the sword. At least 69 people have been beheaded this year in Saudi Arabia for crimes including murder.

According to Islamic sharia law enforced in the kingdom, the victim's family may demand the death penalty if the court finds the women guilty and says capital punishment is appropriate. The Gilfords, represented by Yvonne's brother Frank, have said they prefer the maximum sentence.

Hejailan said the nurses' families would travel to Saudi Arabia on Friday to see the women and perhaps attend the trial. The two are in prison in Dammam, near Dhahran. Hejailan said they were in good health.

"I am meeting with the families tomorrow (Thursday) in London. Then they will fly to Saudi Arabia on Friday for their fourth visit. They will see the girls on Saturday, and hopefully on Sunday and Monday as well," Hejailan said.

The case has stirred up controversy since the women were arrested in December, sparking calls for a more open trial. Journalists are barred from the court, but Saudi officials have said the women have nothing to fear if they are innocent.

The proceedings took a surprise twist on Monday when Parry and McLauchlan issued a statement through Hejailan's law firm saying they intended to bring a $200 million suit against the law firm representing the victim's family.

"Once this case has been concluded in Saudi Arabia, and God willing our innocence is established, we intend to bring suit against the American law firm of the Gilford family, Jones Day, for damages in the amount of $200 million," the women said.
They accused the firm of being inaccurate, "inflaming passions" and causing them "tremendous suffering".

The Gilfords are represented by the International Law Firm (ILF) in Riyadh, which is associated with the Cleveland, Ohio-based firm of Jones, Day, Reavis and Pogue. Jones Day is one of the largest law firms in the United States.
ILF said it had no comment on the threatened law suit.
